description: How naturalistic acting and physical-theatre movement coexist in Bovell's hybrid play.
content_html:
A Hybrid Form

Things I Know to Be True is one of very few GCSE set plays that is genuinely hybrid in its theatrical form: it was written to be performed using two distinct and historically separate performance traditions in the same production. The naturalistic family scenes draw on Stanislavskian acting principles. The movement sequences were developed in collaboration with Frantic Assembly and draw on physical theatre practice. Understanding both traditions and — crucially — how they interact in this play is the foundation of the practitioner-application question for this unit.

This is not a case of two traditions accidentally colliding. Bovell wrote the play specifically with Scott Graham of Frantic Assembly as a creative partner; the movement sequences are not added after the fact but are built into the dramatic structure. The result is a form where the transitions between registers — from dialogue to movement, from naturalism to physical abstraction — carry meaning in themselves. Understanding when and why those transitions happen is as important as understanding each tradition in isolation.

Key Fact

Things I Know to Be True uses two traditions deliberately: Stanislavskian emotional truth for the naturalistic dialogue scenes, and Frantic Assembly physical theatre for the movement sequences. Both are structural, not decorative. A student who treats the movement as ‘extra’ misses half the play’s theatrical language.

Stanislavski and the Price Family

Konstantin Stanislavski (1863–1938) developed a systematic approach to actor training that changed the way realistic drama is performed. His central insight was that truthful acting comes from the actor understanding the character’s inner life: their history, desires, relationships, and the specific circumstances of the scene. He called this the given circumstances. For a performer playing any member of the Price family, the given circumstances are richly specified by Bovell: each character’s profession, their history with each other, the year they are having, the specific weight they carry into each scene.

Stanislavski also asked actors to pursue an objective in every scene — a specific, playable goal that the character is trying to achieve. For Bob in the garden scenes, his objective might be simply “to keep this world intact” — to maintain the order and beauty of the space as a counterweight to the disorder his children keep introducing. For Fran in the kitchen confrontations, her objective might be “to make my child tell me the truth” or “to protect this family from what is coming.” When a performer anchors their choices to a clear objective, every physical and vocal decision becomes purposeful: it is always in the service of getting what the character wants.

For the performer playing Mark, whose arc moves towards his identity as Mia, Stanislavski’s given circumstances are particularly important. The examiner rewards sensitive, specific choices that are grounded in who this character is in relation to this family. The given circumstances include: Mark’s relationship with his parents (the particular emotional dynamic of each parent); his sense of what the revelation will mean for the family; the specific setting (the kitchen or the garden, indoors or out, the season); and the circumstances that immediately precede the scene. A Stanislavskian performer does not play a generalised “coming out scene” — they play this character, in this moment, with these specific people. The choices that come from that specificity are always more compelling, and more mark-worthy, than the generic ones.

Frantic Assembly: Physical Theatre as Emotional Language

Frantic Assembly was founded in 1994 by Scott Graham, Steven Hoggett and Vicki Middleton. The company’s physical theatre practice is distinctive in that it is not primarily dance: it grows from everyday movement — the physicality of ordinary people — and heightens it into something expressive. Their key techniques include round-by-through-under sequences, contact lifts, and chair duets. Scott Graham was the co-director of the original production with Geordie Brookman, contributing movement direction specifically shaped around the Price family’s emotional dynamics.

What makes Frantic Assembly’s approach relevant to Things I Know to Be True specifically is their philosophical starting point: movement should communicate what words cannot. In the context of this play, this translates directly to the moments of greatest emotional intensity. When Bob and a child cannot speak to each other directly about what is happening, Bovell gives them a movement sequence instead. The sequence does not illustrate the conversation; it replaces it with something more honest. A chair duet between Bob and Rosie, for instance, might communicate across several minutes of movement everything that a two-page conversation between them could not.

Key Fact

Frantic Assembly’s key techniques in this play: chair duets (two performers using chairs as contact-improvisation props, expressing relationship through shared weight and negotiated movement); lifts (one performer carrying or lifting another, expressing both protection and the effort of love); and round-by-through-under sequences (continuous, flowing movement through each other’s bodies, suggesting emotional entanglement). None of these are decorative; all are structurally placed to replace dialogue at the point where dialogue fails.

The Moment of Transition: Moving Between Registers

The most interesting theatrical moments in Things I Know to Be True are the transitions: the point where naturalistic dialogue ends and a movement sequence begins, or where a movement sequence dissolves back into dialogue. How does a company signal to the audience that the register is changing? And how does a designer support those transitions?

In production, these transitions are typically managed through a combination of sound, lighting and the performers’ own physical approach to stillness. The dialogue scene reaches its emotional peak — a phrase, a silence, a look — and then the movement begins, often initiated by a single performer before the others join. A sound designer might cue a shift in the soundscape: the domestic acoustic of the kitchen falls away and a non-diegetic, texturally abstract underscore takes its place. A lighting designer might allow the lighting state to shift slightly: the movement sequences often benefit from a reduction in overall intensity, with one or two moving lights following the performers, so that the space feels different — more interior, more subjective — than it does during the dialogue scenes. When the movement ends and dialogue resumes, the lighting returns, the soundscape resolves, and the audience is brought back to the domestic world they were in before.

Stanislavski’s system asks: what does this character want? What are their given circumstances? How does their past shape this moment? It starts from the inside — from the character’s inner life — and works outward to the physical expression of that inner life. The result, when it works, is a performance that appears effortlessly truthful: the words and the body seem to arise from the same source.

Frantic Assembly’s approach asks: what does this body do? How do two bodies relate to each other in space? What does shared weight communicate that words cannot? It starts from the outside — from physical contact and spatial relationship — and works inward. The performers are not asked to “feel something and show it”; they are asked to execute a precise physical task, and the feeling arises from the task. This is in some ways the inverse of Stanislavski’s method, yet in Things I Know to Be True the two approaches are placed alongside each other in the same production and the same family, and they reinforce rather than contradict each other. The Stanislavskian given circumstances of the Price family give the Frantic Assembly movement sequences their specific emotional charge; the movement sequences, in turn, reveal the subterranean emotional life that Stanislavskian truth keeps below the surface of the dialogue.
exam_tip_html:
For any question that asks you to apply practitioner techniques to this play, you must do more than describe the practitioner’s biography. Examiners are looking for the technique applied to a specific moment of the set play. The pattern to follow is: name the practitioner, name the technique, name the moment in the play where it applies, and explain what the technique achieves for the audience at that moment. For example: “Frantic Assembly’s chair-duet technique could be applied to the moment when Bob and a child are unable to speak directly to each other — the shared weight and negotiated movement of the duet communicates the effort of their relationship without any dialogue needing to name it, creating an emotional honesty the naturalistic scene cannot reach.”

For the 20-mark extended staging response, a question about practitioner application is also a staging question: you must address how the technique manifests in performance AND how a designer supports it. The movement sequence and the lighting state that accompanies it are part of the same theatrical statement. Do not describe one without the other.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Things I Know to Be True uses two traditions in deliberate combination: Stanislavskian acting for the naturalistic dialogue scenes (given circumstances, objectives, emotional truth) and Frantic Assembly physical theatre for the movement sequences (chair duets, lifts, round-by-through-under). Both are built into the structure, not added as decoration.
  • Stanislavski starts from the inside (inner life, given circumstances) and works outward; Frantic Assembly starts from the outside (physical task, shared weight) and works inward. In this play, the two approaches reinforce each other: Stanislavskian truth charges the movement with specific emotional meaning; the movement reveals what the dialogue keeps below the surface.
  • The transitions between registers — dialogue to movement, movement back to dialogue — are supported by sound and lighting design. A soundscape shift and a change in lighting state signal to the audience that the register has changed. Every transition is a design opportunity.

practice_questions.text: Name the Frantic Assembly co-director who worked with Andrew Bovell to develop Things I Know to Be True.
What is meant by 'given circumstances' in Stanislavski's acting approach?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying given circumstances as information about a character's situation (who they are, where they are, when the scene takes place); 1 mark for explaining how given circumstances guide a performer's choices (they provide the specific context from which truthful action arises, shaping objectives and motivations).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Frantic Assembly's physical theatre techniques communicate emotional content that the naturalistic dialogue scenes in Things I Know to Be True cannot reach on their own.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of Frantic Assembly's starting point (physical task rather than emotional display) (1); explanation of how this externalises subtext (shared weight and movement communicates what characters feel but cannot say) (1); reference to a specific technique (chair duet, lift, round-by-through-under) (1); explanation of the effect on the audience when the register shifts from dialogue to movement (the audience reads the physical interaction as emotional truth) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Rosie in a Frantic Assembly movement sequence with Bob, explain the specific physical approach you would take to communicate the relationship between daughter and father. What would your choices of weight-sharing, spatial proximity and pace of movement communicate to the audience?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific physical choices for the Frantic Assembly sequence: weight-sharing described in detail (e.g. beginning with Rosie offering her weight to Bob and him accepting it, establishing a physical trust; later in the sequence, Bob initiating a lift that Rosie resists slightly before yielding, suggesting the complexity of the relationship); spatial proximity managed carefully (close enough to communicate intimacy; not so close that it becomes claustrophobic, preserving the sense that this is a father and daughter rather than two people in crisis); pace of movement: beginning slower and increasing as the sequence builds, then resolving to stillness, so that the emotional trajectory is felt in the body before it is understood by the mind. Every choice anchored to the specific emotional content of the father-daughter relationship.

Secure: At least two specific physical choices for the sequence with justification; both anchored to the father-daughter relationship; audience effect present. May not achieve the precision of Mastering.

Developing: General movement ideas (e.g. 'we would move slowly and carefully'); limited specificity; audience effect implied.

Emerging: Describes the movement sequence without specific physical choices; no clear link to the father-daughter relationship.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would use a change in lighting state to support the transition from a naturalistic dialogue scene into a Frantic Assembly movement sequence in Things I Know to Be True. Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience's experience of the moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific lighting state described for the dialogue scene (e.g. a naturalistic interior warm wash, Fresnel cover from above, no moving lights, a sense of domestic ordinariness). Transition: a gradual dimming of the general wash (3-5 seconds) as the movement sequence begins, paired with the activation of one or two moving lights that track the performers, removing them from the fixed domestic world; gel shifts to a cooler, slightly less saturated tone (e.g. from warm 3000K to a neutral or slightly blue-tinted 4000K equivalent) to signal the shift to a more interior, subjective register. Return: the reverse at the sequence's end — the moving lights fade, the domestic wash returns, the gobo (if used for the garden) reinstates. Every choice explained with its effect on the audience.

Secure: At least two named lighting choices for the transition; both explained with audience effect; at least one named element (lantern type, gel colour, intensity). May not achieve the full precision of Mastering.

Developing: Lighting changes described in general terms ('I would dim the lights'); one or two choices; effect implied.

Emerging: Mention of lighting with no specific elements; no clear link to the transition moment.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging a scene from Things I Know to Be True that uses both Stanislavskian naturalistic dialogue and a Frantic Assembly movement sequence, explain how you would direct the performers across both registers and how the design would support the transition between them. Refer to specific practitioner techniques, performer choices and at least two design disciplines.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both practitioners addressed with specific techniques. Stanislavski: the performer is anchored in given circumstances for the dialogue scene (specific objective named, e.g. Bob trying to hold the family together; specific physical grounding, e.g. hands in the soil, a physical task that is then released at the emotional peak). Frantic Assembly: the movement sequence described with named vocabulary (round-by-through-under, shared weight, a lift); the emotional content the sequence communicates named and justified. Design: lighting state for dialogue vs movement sequence (specific choices per phase); soundscape transition (diegetic domestic sounds for the dialogue; abstract underscore for the movement; return to diegetic on resolution). Costume contributes to the reading of the movement (e.g. a fabric that moves well, or a contrast between a character who is dressed more formally and one who moves with greater physical freedom). Every choice justified with reference to audience effect.

Secure: Both practitioners addressed; at least two design disciplines; specific choices made with justification. May not achieve the full integration of Mastering.

Developing: Both practitioners mentioned but not applied to specific moments; design present but general; audience effect implied.

Emerging: One practitioner only, or both practitioners described biographically without application to the staging task.

knowledge_checks.q: What is Stanislavski's term for all the information about a character's situation that the actor must understand?
Which of the following best describes Frantic Assembly's approach to creating movement?
options: Starting from the character's inner emotional life and expressing it through movement
Starting from a physical task or contact-improvisation and letting emotion arise from that
Teaching performers a fixed choreographic sequence and repeating it precisely
Using traditional dance vocabulary adapted for dramatic contexts

knowledge_checks.q: In Stanislavski's system, the overall goal a character is pursuing throughout the entire play is called their _____.
The Frantic Assembly technique in which performers pass through each other in a continuous flowing sequence is called _____.
Match each practitioner to their starting point in creating performance:
right: Starts from the character's inner life, given circumstances and objective
Starts from physical task and contact improvisation; feeling arises from the task

flashcard_questions.a: A method of truthful, internally motivated performance grounded in given circumstances and character objectives.
Theatre in which movement and physical expression are as central as spoken text.

flashcard_questions.q: What are given circumstances in Stanislavski's system?
flashcard_questions.a: All information about a character's situation: who, where, when and what has happened before.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an objective in Stanislavski's system?
flashcard_questions.a: The overall goal a character is pursuing throughout the play or scene.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was the Frantic Assembly co-director who co-developed Things I Know to Be True with Bovell?
What is a chair duet in Frantic Assembly's vocabulary?
flashcard_questions.a: Two performers using chairs as contact-improvisation props to create lifts, slides and counter-balances.
A Frantic Assembly technique in which performers pass through each other in a continuous flowing sequence.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a Frantic Assembly movement sequence replace in this play?
flashcard_questions.a: Naturalistic dialogue at moments of emotional intensity — it externalises what words cannot contain.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between Stanislavski and Frantic Assembly as starting points for performance?
flashcard_questions.a: Stanislavski starts from inner life; Frantic Assembly starts from physical task.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a sound designer support the transition from dialogue to movement in this play?
flashcard_questions.a: By shifting from diegetic domestic sounds to a non-diegetic, abstract underscore as movement begins.
The quality, colour and intensity of all active lights on stage at a given moment.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do both Stanislavski and Frantic Assembly reinforce each other in this play?
flashcard_questions.a: Stanislavskian truth charges the movement with emotional specificity; movement reveals what dialogue suppresses.

glossary_terms.definition: A theatrical style pioneered by Konstantin Stanislavski that seeks truthful, internally motivated performance, grounding character in specific given circumstances and emotional authenticity.

A form of theatre in which movement and physical expression are as important as, or more important than, spoken text, often using contact improvisation, ensemble dynamics and non-naturalistic gesture.
Stanislavski's term for all the information about a character's situation: who they are, where they are, when the scene takes place, and what has happened before.
Stanislavski's term for the overall goal a character is pursuing throughout the entire play; the driving desire that shapes all their actions.
A Frantic Assembly movement technique in which two or more performers pass through each other's bodies in a continuous flowing sequence, creating a sense of fluidity and emotional entanglement.
A Frantic Assembly technique in which two performers use chairs as contact-improvisation props to create a sequence of lifts, slides, counter-balances and shared weight.
A continuous ambient sound environment constructed from multiple elements, used to create place and emotional atmosphere.
The quality, colour and intensity of light on stage at a given moment, created by the combination of all active lanterns.
